keyVerseText: Thus saith the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel, and his Holy One, to him whom man despiseth, to him whom the nation abhorreth, to a servant of rulers, Kings shall see and arise, princes also shall worship, because of the LORD that is faithful, and the Holy One of Israel, and he shall choose thee. whom man: or, that is despised in soul
rootMeaning: The root of בָּזֹה (bâzôh) is בָּזָה (bâzâh), which conveys the fundamental sense of despising or holding something or someone in contempt. This root captures not only the act of despising but also the state of being regarded as vile or worthless, emphasizing a deep disesteem. Unlike the simple English term 'despise,' the Hebrew root carries a layered meaning that includes both the internal attitude of contempt and the external expression of scorn toward a person or thing.
usageInScripture: The word בָּזֹה occurs only once in Scripture, translated as 'despiseth' in Isaiah 49:7. This limited usage underscores its specific and weighty meaning, consistently reflecting an attitude of scorn or rejection by others. The singular occurrence highlights the term's focus on the experience of being despised, rather than a broad range of contemptuous behaviors, emphasizing the personal and relational dimension of disdain in the biblical context.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding בָּזֹה deepens our grasp of the human condition as portrayed in Scripture, where being despised is not merely social rejection but a profound spiritual reality. It reveals the pain and isolation experienced by those whom society rejects, a condition Jesus Himself identified with in His earthly ministry. This word invites believers to reflect on the faithfulness of God toward those who are despised, affirming that God's redeeming work elevates and honors the rejected. It challenges the Christian community to recognize and uphold the dignity of those scorned by the world, reflecting the heart of Christ who was despised yet faithful.
keyVerseReflection: Isaiah 49:7 speaks of the LORD as the Redeemer who addresses 'him whom man despiseth,' highlighting the experience of being scorned by humanity. The use of בָּזֹה here brings out the depth of rejection faced by the servant of rulers, yet it is precisely this despised one whom God chooses and honors. This word enriches the verse by emphasizing that God's faithfulness and holiness are made manifest through lifting up those whom society rejects, assuring believers that divine approval surpasses human scorn.
